newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian rebels say could step up attacks.
newsitem.headline: Colombian rebels say could step up attacks.

text.p: A leftist rebel leader warned on Wednesday he was ready to step up attacks on the military and take more hostages if necessary, just days after freeing 60 soldiers he held for nine months.

Speaking to Reuters in his jungle camp, Comrade Joaquin Gomez, commander of the Southern Block of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), also expressed doubts about the government's commitment to start talks to end Colombia's 3-decade-old internal conflict.

"One begins with small things and works up. The attack (in which the soldiers were captured) has opened the door to attacks on much larger military targets, though that doesn't mean we will ignore the little ones," Gomez said.

"If the conflict continues then ... there could come a moment when the capture of hostages could create a different type of opportunity (for us)," he added, cradling his Russian-made AK-47 assault rifle.

The FARC captured the 60 soldiers and killed 31 others in a raid on the base at Las Delicias in neighbouring Putumayo province last August. The raid, one of the heaviest defeats ever dealt to the military, began Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis, which was largely overshadowed by the recent Japanese embassy residence siege in Peru.

The troops, together with 10 marines captured in a separate firefight in northwest Choco province in January, were released on Sunday in the town of Cartagena del Chaira, at the heart of a 5,000-square-mile (13,000 sq km) zone that the government demilitarized for 32 days for the handover.

Gomez described the attack and subsequent release process as being of "transcendental" importance, demonstrating the FARC's growing tactical prowess and its developing political savvy in the way it forced the army to pull out of the area.
Catholic Church leaders and government officials have speculated the handover could jump start peace negotiations, but Gomez warned against overoptimism.

"In a class society a single word can have two meanings depending on which class uses it. For the ruling class peace means the ability to continue enjoying their belongings ... to continue exploiting the people," he said. "But our understanding of peace is social justice."

President Ernesto Samper reiterated his call for peace but said "these are processes that take years" in radio interviews this week. "It's not that we're losing the war but we're not winning it, we've been in a status quo for many years ... in which innocent people are getting the worst of things," he said.

In a communique that Gomez read at Sunday's handover, the FARC's supreme commander Manuel "Sureshot" Marulanda laid down a series of conditions for future peace talks including an end to repression of grassroots movements and demilitarization of other parts of the country.
Army top brass, however, appeared to have slammed the door on any possibility of an accord with the guerrillas.
